questions.q: A script that worked from your laptop at home now times out on the client's network. The code has not changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: The API has switched from JSON to HTML responses
Python needs reinstalling on the client network
The network path is different, such as a proxy or firewall blocking outbound calls
DNS only works on home networks
questions.why: Inside a company, requests pass through VPNs, proxies and firewalls, so a working call can fail because of the network path, not the code.

questions.q: An API call returns status 503. Where should you look first?
options: The server side, because 5xx means the server failed
Your request body, because 5xx means you sent bad data
Your API key, because 5xx means not authenticated
The page address, because 5xx means not found
questions.why: The 5xx family means the other side has a problem, while 4xx points back at what you sent.

questions.q: A client says they changed a page but users still see the old version. The response shows cf-cache-status: HIT. What is the best first explanation?
options: The deploy failed and must be redone
The server rejected the request with an error
DNS is pointing to the wrong IP address
A cached copy is being served, so the request may never reach the original server
The browser does not support HTTP/2
questions.why: HIT means a cached copy was served, and caching is a common reason changes do not appear.

questions.q: Why should a GET request never be used to change data on the server?
options: GET requests cannot carry headers
Browsers, caches and link previews may repeat GET requests
GET requests are always sent without encryption
Servers ignore GET requests that include a path
questions.why: Because GET can be repeated automatically, any change it makes could happen more than once.

questions.q: A script reads amounts from a CSV and finds that '9' is treated as bigger than '10'. What went wrong?
options: csv.DictReader sorts rows in reverse
The values were compared as text and need converting with float() or int()
The file was opened without a with block
The amounts column needs to be a dict
questions.why: CSV values always arrive as text, so numbers must be converted before comparing or adding.

questions.q: Your script stops with KeyError: 'amount'. What is the most likely cause?
options: The file could not be found in the current folder
A value like 'n/a' reached float()
A variable was used before it was created
The column header is spelled differently, has a space, or uses different capitals
Text was added to a number
questions.why: KeyError means the dict has no key with that name, usually a header that does not match exactly.

questions.q: Two projects on your laptop need different versions of the same package. What solves this?
options: A separate virtual environment for each project
Installing both versions into the system Python
Adding the package name to .gitignore
Using json.load instead of the package
Running each script from a different terminal window
questions.why: A virtual environment gives each project its own private folder of packages so versions do not clash.

questions.q: Your script reports 100 records but the client says the system holds 2,400. What is the most likely cause?
options: The API key has expired
The JSON was parsed as text
The script only processed the first page of results
The request had no timeout set
questions.why: If you forget pagination, you silently process only the first page and totals come out wrong.

questions.q: An API call returns 403 with a key you know is valid. What does that tell you?
options: The key is missing from the request
The server has crashed
The endpoint does not exist
The key is recognised but not allowed to do this action
You have sent too many requests
questions.why: A 401 means the key is missing or wrong, while a 403 means it is valid but lacks permission.

questions.q: Your loop gets a 429 response with a Retry-After header. What should the code do?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop until it works
Wait the number of seconds given, retry, and cap the number of retries
Switch to a POST request instead
Stop and treat the data as complete
Remove the Authorization header and try again
questions.why: 429 means too many requests, so you wait as the API asks and limit retries to avoid getting blocked.

questions.q: After joining invoices to another table, the invoice total is higher than before. What should you check first?
options: Whether the table uses REAL or TEXT for amounts
Whether ORDER BY was used
Whether the join key is unique, by counting rows before and after the join
Whether the query used single quotes
Whether HAVING was placed after GROUP BY
questions.why: Joining on a key that is not unique multiplies rows, which inflates totals.

questions.q: You want only suppliers whose total open invoices are above 500. Which clause filters on that total?
options: HAVING, because it filters groups after they are totalled
WHERE, because it filters groups after they are totalled
ORDER BY, because it puts the biggest first
JOIN, because it combines matching rows
questions.why: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters totals after grouping.

questions.q: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT invoice_id) FROM invoices returns 1,050 and 1,000. What does this tell you?
options: There are duplicate invoice rows, so totals built on this table will be wrong
50 invoices have a NULL amount
50 invoices have no matching supplier
The table has 50 more columns than expected
questions.why: If the row count and the distinct key count differ, the key is duplicated.

questions.q: Why use ? placeholders when running SQL from Python?
options: They make queries run faster on large tables
They let SQLite store dates in any format
They keep input text out of the SQL, preventing SQL injection and handling quotes
They turn a JOIN into a LEFT JOIN automatically
They are required for SELECT but not INSERT
questions.why: Placeholders stop input from being mistaken for SQL commands and handle quotes in values.

questions.q: You pushed a file containing an API key yesterday and deleted it today. What should you do?
options: Nothing, the delete commit removed it
Treat the key as leaked: tell the owner, revoke it and create a new one
Add the file to .gitignore and push again
Rename the branch so the old commit is hidden
questions.why: Anything committed stays in history, so deleting the file does not make the key safe.

questions.q: Which file stops Git from tracking .env and local database files?
options: requirements.txt
README
config.json
.gitignore
questions.why: A .gitignore lists file patterns Git should never track, such as .env and *.db.

questions.q: You have a 2,000 line change ready for review. What is the better approach?
options: Push it straight to main to save the reviewer time
Open one pull request with the commit message 'update'
Split it into smaller pull requests that each do one thing
Merge it first and ask for review afterwards
Squash it into one commit so it looks smaller
questions.why: A reviewer can check a small change properly but will only skim a very large one.

questions.q: An assistant's parse_amount function returns 0 for a blank amount. Why is that a problem?
options: It makes the function slower on large files
Python cannot add 0 to a float
Blank amounts should always be treated as negative
It hides bad rows inside a total instead of failing loudly
questions.why: Returning 0 silently guesses, so bad data disappears into totals; raising an error makes it visible.

questions.q: The assistant has failed to fix the same bug twice and each fix breaks something else. What should you do?
options: Stop, clear the session, and write a better first request with the exact error and what you learned
Keep repeating the same request until it works
Accept the latest change and test later
Ask it to change more files at once
Turn off the tests so the changes can go in
questions.why: After repeated failed corrections a fresh session with a clearer request usually works better than pushing on.

questions.q: Before you ask an AI assistant to make a big change across several files, what should you do?
options: Paste some real customer records so it understands the data
Commit your current work so you can see exactly what it changed and undo it
Delete the tests so they do not slow it down
Give it your API keys so it can run everything
questions.why: Git is the safety net: a commit before a big change lets you review the diff and roll back.
